title: Jonah's Gourd Vine
significance: Her first novel, tracing the life of the preacher John Pearson to draw Black church sermon into the sentences of fiction. This is the point where the recorded vernacular and the rhythm of sermon begin to spread beyond dialogue into the narration itself.

title: Mules and Men
significance: Black folktales and hoodoo rituals recorded at Florida logging camps and in New Orleans, woven not into a scholarly report but into a narrative in which the collector herself appears. With a preface by Franz Boas, the book is an early instance of blurring the line between ethnography and literature.

title: Their Eyes Were Watching God
significance: The story of Janie, who finds her own voice across three marriages, written in a free indirect style that mixes standard-English narration with Black Southern vernacular within a single sentence. Written in a matter of weeks while Hurston was in Haiti, the novel entered the canon of American fiction after its 1970s rediscovery.

title: Tell My Horse
significance: A record of fieldwork conducted in Jamaica and Haiti, setting accounts of voodoo ritual and spirit possession alongside the political history of the two countries. Its view of the Caribbean as an extension of Black Southern culture in the United States is cited as a precedent for later Black Atlantic studies.

title: Moses, Man of the Mountain
significance: A novel that reimagines the Exodus figure of Moses as a hoodoo conjure man. It overlays the biblical narrative of liberation on the experience of American slavery and renders the characters' speech in Southern vernacular, placing recorded folk belief and canonical scripture on the same plane.

title: Barracoon: The Story of the Last "Black Cargo"
significance: Based on interviews in the late 1920s with Cudjo Lewis, said to be one of the last survivors of the Atlantic slave trade, the manuscript was completed in 1931 but shelved when Hurston refused a publisher's demand to convert his speech into standard English — it was not published until 2018. A case in which the principle of preserving testimony exactly as spoken blocked publication itself.

title: Invisible Man
significance: A novel in which an unnamed narrator passes from a Southern Black college to Harlem political organizing, embodying in its very narrative form the fact that he is treated by others as invisible. It won the National Book Award the following year and became a benchmark of postwar American fiction.

title: Shadow and Act
significance: A collection of essays on jazz and blues, American folklore, and his own literary education. It includes "The World and the Jug," his rebuttal to criticism that confines Black writers to the role of sociological witness.

title: Going to the Territory
significance: His second essay collection, published some twenty years after the first. It extends his argument that American culture was made through the mutual interpenetration of Black and white, with concrete examples drawn from music, language, and regional history.

title: Juneteenth
significance: A posthumously published edition of the second novel Ellison worked on for more than forty years and left unfinished, edited into a single volume by his literary executor John Callahan. It concerns the relationship between a senator who has lived his life passing as white and a Black minister, and its very status as an edited compilation has itself become a subject of dispute.

title: Go Tell It on the Mountain
significance: Baldwin's first novel, built around a single night in a Harlem Pentecostal church, retracing three generations of a family's conversions and guilt. It is the starting point of Baldwin's style, which carries the sentence rhythms of the King James Bible and the sermon into novelistic prose.

title: Notes of a Native Son
significance: His first essay collection, including the title essay on a day on which his father's funeral coincided with a Harlem riot. Answering Richard Wright's Native Son in its very title, it offers, in the prose itself, his critique that protest fiction reduces Black people to statistical victims.

title: Giovanni's Room
significance: A novel set in Paris, dealing with the relationship between a white American male narrator and an Italian bartender. The choice not to include a single Black character drew objections from his publisher, and the novel became an early instance of treating homosexuality not as pathology or scandal but as a problem of self-deception.

title: Another Country
significance: Beginning with the suicide of a Black jazz drummer, it traces the relationships of those left behind, mapping a terrain where race, class, and sexual orientation intersect among characters who move between Greenwich Village and Harlem. It is the widest in social scope of Baldwin's novels.

title: The Fire Next Time
significance: A book made of two pieces: a short letter to his nephew written on the hundredth anniversary of emancipation, and a long essay on his encounter with Elijah Muhammad of the Nation of Islam. It became a bestseller in the middle of the civil rights movement and installed Baldwin as a public voice.

title: If Beale Street Could Talk
significance: Narrated in the first person by a pregnant nineteen-year-old waiting for the lover imprisoned on a false rape charge, it reconstructs the violence of the criminal justice system within a family's everyday time. It is the only one of Baldwin's novels to use a woman narrator.

title: Wise Blood
significance: Her first novel, depicting how Hazel Motes, back from the army, becomes more trapped within the structure of faith the harder he tries to deny it by founding the 'Church Without Christ.' A structure that runs at the pace of comedy before ending in self-mutilation, which became the skeleton of O'Connor's later fiction.

title: A Good Man Is Hard to Find and Other Stories
significance: A story collection including the title piece, in which a family road trip ends in an encounter with an escaped convict. The standard form of an O'Connor story, proceeding in chatty everyday language before violence overturns everything into an event of recognition in the final paragraphs, is established here.

title: The Violent Bear It Away
significance: Her second novel, following a boy raised to be a prophet as he heads to the city to refuse that calling. As the title, drawn from a verse in the Gospel of Matthew, suggests, it pushes through a structure in which refusing the calling ends up fulfilling it.

title: Everything That Rises Must Converge
significance: A posthumous collection of stories she had chosen up until shortly before her death. Scenes of mothers' and children's generations destroying one another recur across a South where racial segregation was collapsing, and the title comes from a phrase of Teilhard de Chardin.

title: Mystery and Manners: Occasional Prose
significance: A prose collection of lectures and reviews she gave in her lifetime, assembled posthumously by Sally and Robert Fitzgerald. It explains why the Southern grotesque is necessary, and how a Catholic writer should speak to a reader who does not share her faith, treating both as questions of form rather than theme.

title: The Sea Wall
significance: The story of a mother and her two children in French Indochina, after the mother is cheated by the colonial administration into buying land that floods with seawater. The work in which the material of Duras's Indochinese childhood, which she would go on rewriting for the rest of her life, first became fiction; at this point she still uses a narrative form with clear causation.

title: Moderato Cantabile
significance: A short novel that proceeds through nothing but the repeated conversations of a man and a woman about a crime of passion they witnessed at a café. Because it withholds explanation of the event to the very end and leaves behind only dialogue and a count of glasses of wine, it was discussed alongside the nouveau roman from soon after its publication at Éditions de Minuit.

title: Hiroshima mon amour
significance: The screenplay and dialogue Duras wrote for the film Alain Resnais directed in 1959, published as a book the following year. It overlays the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and a private memory from Nevers within the same sentences, attempting a narration that sets historical catastrophe and personal memory as equivalents.

title: The Ravishing of Lol Stein
significance: It follows the later life of a woman whose fiancé is taken from her at a ball, but is written in a structure where the narrator openly admits to inventing scenes he did not witness. After Lacan addressed it in a separate essay, it became a recurring reference point in psychoanalytic criticism.

title: The Lover
significance: It reconstructs, in short paragraphs that keep shifting tense and person, the relationship between a fifteen-year-old girl and a Chinese man that begins on a ferry crossing the Mekong. Winner of the Prix Goncourt and translated into many languages, it is the book that made Duras most widely read.

title: The North China Lover
significance: A late novel that rewrites the same material from the beginning, written amid conflict with Jean-Jacques Annaud's film adaptation. It restores scenes The Lover had omitted and adds stage directions close to shooting instructions, making the rewriting of her own text a working method in itself.

title: The Erasers
significance: Written in the outward form of a detective novel, it follows twenty-four hours in which a police inspector investigating a murder that has not yet happened ends up committing that very murder. His first novel, overlaying the structure of the Oedipus myth not on plot events but on the description of objects.

title: The Voyeur
significance: Written so that, in a day in the life of a watch salesman making his rounds on an island, exactly the span of time corresponding to a girl's death is missing from the narration. This gap, which forces the reader to fill in what is missing, became a basic device of his later fiction, and the novel won the Prix des Critiques after fierce controversy on its publication.

title: Jealousy
significance: In a house on a tropical plantation, only a gaze watching a wife and a neighboring man remains, and the subject of that gaze never once appears as 'I.' A repeating narration that counts the slats of a blind and the rows of banana trees completes a structure that generates jealousy without a single word naming the emotion.

title: In the Labyrinth
significance: It narrates the movements of a soldier who cannot find where to deliver a parcel in a snow-covered city, through paragraphs that repeat the same streets and the same room with small variations. It is the novel from which he most thoroughly removed every clue for reconstructing chronological order.

title: Last Year at Marienbad
significance: The screenplay for the film directed by Alain Resnais, published as a text under the name 'ciné-roman.' Two characters each assert mismatched memories of a meeting the previous year, and the text never settles, to the end, what actually happened.

title: For a New Novel
significance: A collection of essays arguing that Balzacian character, plot, and psychological description should be dropped as requirements of the novel. With the thesis that objects are not vessels for human emotion but simply there, it became a reference point in later debates over the French novel.

title: Wołanie do Yeti
significance: Her third poetry collection, published after she disowned the two early collections she had written in the Socialist Realist period. The title poem is often read as an address to Stalinism, and this is where the tone of irony and questioning that would come to characterize her poetry first appears.

title: Sól
significance: Her fourth poetry collection, gathering poems that take objects and animals as objects of observation to question humanity's place among them. The method of designing a single poem as a single question becomes settled here, and poems that would go on to be repeatedly reprinted in later anthologies begin to appear.

title: Nonrequired Reading
significance: A collection of short columns on books not normally treated as subjects for review — cookbooks, practical manuals, field guides. Carrying over into prose the same irony and digressive logic she used in her poems, she turned the book-review form into a genre of humor.

title: Wielka liczba
significance: The title poem asks how poetry can count a single person against a population in the billions. This is the collection in which her way of pulling the vocabulary of statistics and probability into lyric poetry shows most clearly.

title: People on a Bridge
significance: The title poem takes up the scene, within a Hiroshige woodblock print, of people crossing a bridge in the rain who never arrive, and treats it as art's attempt to stop time. A collection that condenses her later method of pushing a single image all the way through to an ontological question.

title: Koniec i początek
significance: It includes both the title poem, about the people who clear the rubble once a war has ended, and "Cat in an Empty Apartment," written from the point of view of a cat left behind after its owner's death. Published just before the Nobel Prize, it is best known in Korea through an anthology carrying the same title.
